arXiv:math/0401225v3 [math.AG] 14 Sep 2004

Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces

Adrien Dubouloz Address: Adrien Dubouloz
Institut Fourier, Laboratoire de Mathématiques
UMR5582 (UJF-CNRS)
BP 74 St Martin d’Hères Cedex, FRANCE Email address: adrien.dubouloz@ujf-grenoble.fr
Abstract.

We study a class of normal affine surfaces with additive group actions which contains in particular the Danielewski surfaces in 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} given by the equations xn​z=P⁡(y)x^{n}z=P\left(y\right), where PP is a nonconstant polynomial with simple roots. We call them Danielewski-Fieseler Surfaces. We reinterpret a construction of Fieseler [7] to show that these surfaces appear as the total spaces of certain torsors under a line bundle over a curve with an rr-fold point. We classify Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces through labelled rooted trees attached to such a surface in a canonical way. Finally, we characterize those surfaces which have a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant in terms of the associated trees.

2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
14L30,14R05,14R20,14R25

Introduction

The surfaces Sj={xjz=y2+1}S_{j}=\left\{x^{j}z=y^{2}+1\right\}, j≥1j\geq 1, in ℂ3=Spec​(ℂ⁡[x,y,z])\mathbb{C}^{3}=\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x,y,z\right]\right) admit free actions of the additive group 𝔾a,ℂ\mathbb{G}_{a,\mathbb{C}} induced by the locally nilpotent derivations ∂j=xj∂y+2y∂z\partial_{j}=x^{j}\partial_{y}+2y\partial_{z} of ℂ⁡[x,y,z]\mathbb{C}\left[x,y,z\right] respectively. Danielewski [4] observed that the associated quotient morphism π:Sj→Sj//𝔾a,ℂ≃Spec(ℂ[x])\pi:S_{j}\rightarrow S_{j}/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a,\mathbb{C}}\simeq\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]\right) is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration which factors throught an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:Sj→X\rho:S_{j}\rightarrow X over the affine line with a double origin δ:X→Spec​(ℂ​[x])\delta:X\rightarrow\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]\right). Indeed, SjS_{j} is obtained as the gluing of two copies Spec​(ℂ​[x]​[Ti])\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]\left[T_{i}\right]\right) of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, i=1,2i=1,2, over ℂ∗×ℂ\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C} by means of the ℂ​[x]x\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]_{x}-algebras isomorphisms ℂ​[x]x​[T1]→∼ℂ​[x]x​[T2]\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]_{x}\left[T_{1}\right]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]_{x}\left[T_{2}\right], T1↦2​x−j+T2T_{1}\mapsto 2x^{-j}+T_{2}. This interpretation was further generalized by Fieseler [7] to describe certain invariant neighbourhoods of the fibers of a quotient 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:S→Z\pi:S\rightarrow Z associated with a nontrivial action of 𝔾a,ℂ\mathbb{G}_{a,\mathbb{C}} on a normal affine surface SS. More precisely, he established that if a fiber π−1​(z0)\pi^{-1}\left(z_{0}\right) is reduced then the induced morphism p2:S×ZSpec​(𝒪Z,z0)→Spec​(𝒪Z,z0)p_{2}:S\times_{Z}\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathcal{O}_{Z,z_{0}}\right)\rightarrow\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathcal{O}_{Z,z_{0}}\right), where 𝒪Z,z0\mathcal{O}_{Z,z_{0}} denotes the local ring of z0∈Zz_{0}\in Z, factors through an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle ρ:S→X\rho:S\rightarrow X over the scheme XX obtained from Spec​(𝒪Z,z0)\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathcal{O}_{Z,z_{0}}\right) by replacing z0z_{0} by as many points as there are connected components in π−1​(z0)\pi^{-1}\left(z_{0}\right). More generally, given a field kk of caracteristic zero and a pair (X=Spec​(A),x0=div​(x))\left(X=\textrm{Spec}\left(A\right),x_{0}=\textrm{div}\left(x\right)\right), where AA is either discrete valuation ring with uniformizing parameter xx and residue field kk or of a polynomial ring A=k⁡[x]A=k\left[x\right], the same description holds for the following class of surfaces.

Definition 0.1.

A Danielewski-Fieseler surface with base (A,x)\left(A,x\right) (A DFS, for short) is an integral affine XX-scheme π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X of finite type, restricting to a trivial line bundle over X∗=X∖{x0}X_{*}=X\setminus\left\{x_{0}\right\}, and such that π−1​(x0)\pi^{-1}\left(x_{0}\right) is nonempty and reduced, consisting of a disjoint union of curves isomorphic to affine line 𝔸k1\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1}.

In this paper, we give a combinatorial description of DFS’s in terms of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled rooted trees, that is, pairs γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) consisting of a rooted tree Γ\Gamma and a cochain σ∈An\sigma\in A^{n}, indexed by the terminal elements of Γ\Gamma, satisfying certain conditions with respect to the geometry of Γ\Gamma (see (1.5) below). Then, as an application, we characterize the DFS’s with base (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right) which have a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant [10].

The paper is divided as follows. In section 11, we collect some preliminary results on labelled rooted trees. In section 22, we reinterpret the ’cocycle construction’ of Fieseler [7] to describe DFS’s as torsors under certain line bundles on a nonseparated scheme. In section 33, we associate to every labelled tree γ\gamma, a DFS πγ:S⁡(γ)→X\pi_{\gamma}:S\left(\gamma\right)\rightarrow X which comes equipped with a canonical birational XX-morphism ψγ:S⁡(γ)→𝔸X1\psi_{\gamma}:S\left(\gamma\right)\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{X}^{1}. For instance, given a polynomial P∈k⁡[y]P\in k\left[y\right] with simple roots y1,…,yn∈ky_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\in k, the Danielewski-Fieseler surface with base (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)

π:SP,m=Spec​(k⁡[x,y,z]/(xm​z−P⁡(y)))⟶X=Spec​(k⁡[x]),\pi:S_{P,m}=\textrm{Spec}\left(k\left[x,y,z\right]/\left(x^{m}z-P\left(y\right)\right)\right)\longrightarrow X=\textrm{Spec}\left(k\left[x\right]\right),

equipped with the morphism p​ry:SP,m→𝔸X1=Spec​(k⁡[x]​[y])pr_{y}:S_{P,m}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{X}^{1}=\textrm{Spec}\left(k\left[x\right]\left[y\right]\right) corresponds to the following labelled tree γP,m=(Γm,n,σ)\gamma_{P,m}=\left(\Gamma_{m,n},\sigma\right).

In Theorem (3.2), we establish that the category 𝔇→(A,x)\overrightarrow{\mathfrak{D}}_{\left(A,x\right)} of DFS’s with base (A,x)\left(A,x\right) equipped with certain birational morphisms as above and the category 𝒯(A,x)\mathcal{T}_{\left(A,x\right)} of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees are equivalent. Then, in Theorem (3.10), we classify these DFS’s up to XX-isomorphisms in terms of the corresponding trees. In section 44, we decompose birational XX-morphisms between two DFS’s into a succession of simple affine modifications [11], which we call fibered modifications (Theorem 4.5). This leads to a canonical procedure for constructing embeddings of a DFS π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X into a projective XX-scheme π¯:S¯→X\bar{\pi}:\bar{S}\rightarrow X (Proposition 4.7). Section 55 is devoted to the study of DFS’s with base (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right), which we call simply Danielewski surfaces. We recall that the Makar-Limanov invariant [10] of an affine variety V/kV/k is defined as the intersection in Γ⁡(V,𝒪V)\Gamma\left(V,\mathcal{O}_{V}\right) of all the invariant rings of 𝔾a,k\mathbb{G}_{a,k}-actions on VV. Makar-Limanov [12] and [13] established that a surface SP,m≃S⁡(γP,m)S_{P,m}\simeq S\left(\gamma_{P,m}\right) as above has trivial Makar-Limanov invariant ML​(SP,m)=k\textrm{ML}\left(S_{P,m}\right)=k if and only if m=1m=1 and deg⁡(P)≥1\deg\left(P\right)\geq 1. More generally, in case that k=k¯k=\bar{k} is algebraically closed, we give the following characterization (Theorem 5.4).

Theorem 0.2.

A Danielewski surface S⁡(γ)S\left(\gamma\right) has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant if and only if γ\gamma is a comb, i.e a labelled tree γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) with the property that all but at most one of the direct descendants of a given e∈Γe\in\Gamma are terminal elements of Γ\Gamma.

Finally, we obtain the following description of normal affine surfaces with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant, which generalizes previous results obtained by Daigle-Russell [3] and Miyanishi-Masuda [14] for the particular case of log ℚ\mathbb{Q}-homology planes (Theorem 5.9).

Theorem 0.3.

Every normal affine surface S/k¯S/\bar{k} with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant is isomorphic to a cyclic quotient of a Danielewski surface.

1. Preliminaries on rooted trees

Here we give some results on rooted trees and labelled rooted trees which will be used in the following sections.

Basic facts on rooted trees

Let (G,≤)\left(G,\leq\right) be a nonempty, finite, partially ordered set (a poset, for short). A totally ordered subset C⊂GC\subset G is called a subchain of length l​(C)=Card​(C)−1l\left(C\right)=\textrm{Card}\left(C\right)-1. A subchain of maximal length is called a maximal subchain. For every e∈Ge\in G, we let (↑e)G={e′∈G,e′≥e}\left(\uparrow e\right)_{G}=\left\{e^{\prime}\in G,e^{\prime}\geq e\right\} and (↓e)G={e′∈G,e′≤e}\left(\downarrow e\right)_{G}=\left\{e^{\prime}\in G,e^{\prime}\leq e\right\}. The edges E⁡(G)E\left(G\right) of GG are the subsets e​e′→={e′<e}\overrightarrow{ee^{\prime}}=\left\{e^{\prime}<e\right\} of GG with two elements such that (↑e′)G∩(↓e)G=e​e′→\left(\uparrow e^{\prime}\right)_{G}\cap\left(\downarrow e\right)_{G}=\overrightarrow{ee^{\prime}}.

Definition 1.1.

A (rooted) tree Γ\Gamma is poset with a unique minimal element e0e_{0} called the root, and such that (↓e)Γ\left(\downarrow e\right)_{\Gamma} is a chain for every e∈Γe\in\Gamma. A (rooted) subtree of Γ\Gamma is a sub-poset Γ′⊂Γ\Gamma^{\prime}\subset\Gamma which is a rooted tree for the induced order. We say that Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is maximal if there exists e′∈Γe^{\prime}\in\Gamma such that Γ′=(↑e′)Γ\Gamma^{\prime}=\left(\uparrow e^{\prime}\right)_{\Gamma}.

1.2.

An element e∈Γe\in\Gamma such that l​(↓e)Γ=ml\left(\downarrow e\right)_{\Gamma}=m is said to be at level mm. The maximal elements ei=ei,mie_{i}=e_{i,m_{i}}, where mi=l​(↓ei)Γm_{i}=l\left(\downarrow e_{i}\right)_{\Gamma}, of Γ\Gamma are called the leaves of Γ\Gamma. We denote the set of those elements by L⁡(Γ)L\left(\Gamma\right). The corresponding subchains

(1) (↓ei,mi)Γ={ei,0=e0<ei,1<⋯<ei,mi−1<ei,mi=ei},i=1,…,n.\left(\downarrow e_{i,m_{i}}\right)_{\Gamma}=\left\{e_{i,0}=e_{0}<e_{i,1}<\cdots<e_{i,m_{i}-1}<e_{i,m_{i}}=e_{i}\right\},\quad i=1,\ldots,n.

are the maximal subchains of Γ\Gamma. We say that Γ\Gamma has height h⁡(Γ)=max⁡(mi)h\left(\Gamma\right)=\max\left(m_{i}\right). The first common ancestor of two element e,e′∈Γ∖{e0}e,e^{\prime}\in\Gamma\setminus\left\{e_{0}\right\} is the maximal element of the chain ((↓e)Γ∖{e})∩((↓e′)Γ∖{e′})\left(\left(\downarrow e\right)_{\Gamma}\setminus\left\{e\right\}\right)\cap\left(\left(\downarrow e^{\prime}\right)_{\Gamma}\setminus\left\{e^{\prime}\right\}\right). The children of e∈Γ∖L⁡(Γ)e\in\Gamma\setminus L\left(\Gamma\right) are the minimal elements of (↑e)Γ∖{e}\left(\uparrow e\right)_{\Gamma}\setminus\left\{e\right\}. We denote the set of those elements by ChΓ​(e)\textrm{Ch}_{\Gamma}\left(e\right).

Definition 1.3.

A morphism of (rooted) trees is an order-preserving map τ:Γ′→Γ\tau:\Gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\Gamma satisfying the following properties:

 a) The image of a maximal chain of Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} by τ\tau is a maximal chain of Γ\Gamma.

 b) For every e′∈Γ′e^{\prime}\in\Gamma^{\prime}, τ−1​(τ⁡(e′))\tau^{-1}\left(\tau\left(e^{\prime}\right)\right) is either e′e^{\prime} itself or a maximal subtree of Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}.

Injective and bijective morphisms are referred to as embeddings and isomorphisms respectively.

1.4.

This definition implies that for every leaf ei,mi′′e^{\prime}_{i,m_{i}^{\prime}} of Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} at level mi′m^{\prime}_{i}, τ⁡(ei,mi′′)\tau\left(e^{\prime}_{i,m_{i}^{\prime}}\right) is a leaf ej⁡(i),mj⁡(i)e_{j\left(i\right),m_{j\left(i\right)}} of Γ\Gamma at level mj⁡(i)≤mi′m_{j\left(i\right)}\leq m^{\prime}_{i}, such that τ⁡(ei,k′)=ej⁡(i),min⁡(k,mj⁡(i))\tau\left(e^{\prime}_{i,k}\right)=e_{j\left(i\right),\min\left(k,m_{j\left(i\right)}\right)} for every k=0,…,mi′k=0,\ldots,m^{\prime}_{i} (see (1) for the notation).

Labelled rooted trees

In this subsection, we fix a pair (A,x)\left(A,x\right) consisting of a domain AA and an element x∈A∖{0}x\in A\setminus\left\{0\right\}.

Definition 1.5.

An (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled tree is a pair γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) consisting of a a tree Γ\Gamma with the leaves e1,m1,…,en,mne_{1,m_{1}},\ldots,e_{n,m_{n}} and a cochain σ={σi}i=1,…,n∈An\sigma=\left\{\sigma_{i}\right\}_{i=1,\ldots,n}\in A^{n} such that σj−σi∈xdi​j​A∖xdi​j+1​A\sigma_{j}-\sigma_{i}\in x^{d_{ij}}A\setminus x^{d_{ij}+1}A whenever the first common ancestor of ei,mie_{i,m_{i}} and ej,mje_{j,m_{j}} is at level di​j<min⁡(mi,mj)d_{ij}<\min\left(m_{i},m_{j}\right). A cochain σ\sigma with this this property is said to be Γ\Gamma-compatible.

A morphism of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees τ:(Γ′,σ′)→(Γ,σ)\tau:\left(\Gamma^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}\right)\rightarrow\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) is a morphism of trees τ:Γ′→Γ\tau:\Gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\Gamma such that if ej⁡(i),mj⁡(i)∈L⁡(Γ)e_{j\left(i\right),m_{j\left(i\right)}}\in L\left(\Gamma\right) is the image of a leaf ei,mi′′∈L⁡(Γ′)e^{\prime}_{i,m^{\prime}_{i}}\in L\left(\Gamma^{\prime}\right) by τ\tau, then σi−σj⁡(i)∈xmj⁡(i)​A\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{j\left(i\right)}\in x^{m_{j\left(i\right)}}A.

The category of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled just defined is denoted by 𝒯(A,x)\mathcal{T}_{\left(A,x\right)}.

Example 1.6.

Every isomorphism class of (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled trees contains a tree γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) with the leaves e1,m1,…,en,mne_{1,m_{1}},\ldots,e_{n,m_{n}}, such that σi=∑j=0mi−1wi,j​xj∈k⁡[x]\sigma_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{m_{i}-1}w_{i,j}x^{j}\in k\left[x\right] is a polynomial of degree <mi<m_{i} for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. In turn, this cochain σ\sigma is uniquely determined by the choice of a weight function

wσ:E⁡(Γ)⟶k,ei,j+1​ei,j→↦wσ​(ei,j+1​ei,j→)=wi,jw_{\sigma}:E\left(\Gamma\right)\longrightarrow k,\quad\overrightarrow{e_{i,j+1}e_{i,j}}\mapsto w_{\sigma}\left(\overrightarrow{e_{i,j+1}e_{i,j}}\right)=w_{i,j}

with the property that wσ​(e′​e→)≠wσ​(e′′​e→)w_{\sigma}\left(\overrightarrow{e^{\prime}e}\right)\neq w_{\sigma}\left(\overrightarrow{e^{\prime\prime}e}\right) whenever e′e^{\prime} and e′′e^{\prime\prime} are children of the same e∈Γe\in\Gamma. A tree Γ\Gamma equipped with such a function ww is referred to as a fine kk-weighted tree. A morphism of trees τ:Γ′→Γ\tau:\Gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\Gamma gives rise to a morphism of (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled τ:(Γ′,σ′)→(Γ,σ)\tau:\left(\Gamma^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}\right)\rightarrow\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) if and only if wσ​(τ⁡(e)​τ​(e′)→)=wσ′​(e​e′→)w_{\sigma}\left(\overrightarrow{\tau\left(e\right)\tau\left(e^{\prime}\right)}\right)=w_{\sigma^{\prime}}\left(\overrightarrow{ee^{\prime}}\right)whenever τ⁡(e)≠τ⁡(e′)\tau\left(e\right)\neq\tau\left(e^{\prime}\right). If it is the case, then we say that τ\tau is a morphism of fine kk-weighted trees. In this way, we obtain a bijection between morphisms of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees and morphisms of fine kk-weighted trees. We conclude that the categories 𝒯(k⁡[x],x)\mathcal{T}_{\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)} of (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled trees and 𝒯wk\mathcal{T}_{w}^{k} of fine kk-weighted trees are equivalent.

Gluing trees

Intuitively, (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees are constructed by gluing (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled chains. Similarly, a morphism τ:γ′→γ\tau:\gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\gamma of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees is uniquely determined by its values on maximal subchains of γ′\gamma^{\prime}. More precisely, we have the following results.

Blow-downs of trees

By definition, (see (1.5)), A morphism of trees τ:Γ′→Γ\tau:\Gamma^{\prime}\rightarrow\Gamma factors through the retraction of a collection of maximal subtrees of Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}, followed by an embedding. Therefore, for every element e∈Γ′∖L⁡(Γ′)e\in\Gamma^{\prime}\setminus L\left(\Gamma^{\prime}\right) such that ChΓ′​(e)⊂L⁡(Γ′)\textrm{Ch}_{\Gamma^{\prime}}\left(e\right)\subset L\left(\Gamma^{\prime}\right), the image of the subtree Γe′=(↑e)Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}_{e}=\left(\uparrow e\right)_{\Gamma^{\prime}} of Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is either a subtree τ⁡(Γe′)\tau\left(\Gamma^{\prime}_{e}\right) of Γ\Gamma isomorphic to Γe′\Gamma^{\prime}_{e} or the unique element τ⁡(e)∈L⁡(Γ)\tau\left(e\right)\in L\left(\Gamma\right). In the second case, τ\tau factors through the morphism of trees

Definition 1.9.

Let γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right) be an (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled tree, and let e∈Γ∖L⁡(Γ)e\in\Gamma\setminus L\left(\Gamma\right) be an element such that ChΓ​(e)⊂L​(Γ)\textrm{Ch}_{\Gamma}\left(e\right)\subset L\left(\Gamma\right). A blow-down of the leaves at ee is an (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled tree γ^​(e)=(Γ^​(e),σ^​(e))\hat{\gamma}\left(e\right)=\left(\hat{\Gamma}\left(e\right),\hat{\sigma}\left(e\right)\right) with underlying tree Γ^​(e)=Γ∖ChΓ​(e)\hat{\Gamma}\left(e\right)=\Gamma\setminus\textrm{Ch}_{\Gamma}\left(e\right) for which the morphism of trees τe\tau_{e} above is a morphism of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees τe:γ→γ^​(e)\tau_{e}:\gamma\rightarrow\hat{\gamma}\left(e\right). Since two labelled trees γ^​(e)\hat{\gamma}\left(e\right) with this property are isomorphic, the morphism τe\tau_{e} itself will be usually referred to as the blow-down of the leaves at ee.

As a consequence of the above discussion, we obtain the following description.

Proposition 1.10.

A morphism of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled trees factors into a sequence of blow-downs of leaves followed by an embedding.

whenever ej⁡(i),mj⁡(i)∈L⁡(Es​(Γ))e_{j\left(i\right),m_{j\left(i\right)}}\in L\left(\textrm{Es}\left(\Gamma\right)\right) is the image of ei,mi′′∈L⁡(Es​(Γ′))e^{\prime}_{i,m_{i}^{\prime}}\in L\left(\textrm{Es}\left(\Gamma^{\prime}\right)\right) by τ\tau.

By definition, two essential cochains for a given labelled tree γ\gamma differ by the addition of a constant b∈Ab\in A. Therefore, the essential labelled subtrees for γ\gamma are all equivalent in the sense of definition (1.11).

2. Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces as fiber bundles

To fix the notation, we let kk be a field of caracteristic zero, and we let (A,x)\left(A,x\right) be a pair consisting either of a discrete valuation ring AA with uniformizing parameter xx and residue field kk, or a polynomial ring k⁡[x]k\left[x\right] in one variable xx. We let X=Spec​(A)X=\textrm{Spec}\left(A\right), x0=div​(x)∈Xx_{0}=\textrm{div}\left(x\right)\in X , and we denote by X∗=X∖{x0}≃Spec​(Ax)X_{*}=X\setminus\left\{x_{0}\right\}\simeq\textrm{Spec}\left(A_{x}\right) the open complement of x0x_{0} in XX.

Definition 2.1.

A Danielewski-Fieseler surface (a DFS for short) with base (X,x0)\left(X,x_{0}\right) (or, equivalently, with base (A,x)\left(A,x\right)) is an integral affine XX-scheme π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X of finite type such that S∣X∗S\mid_{X_{*}} is isomorphic to the trivial line bundle 𝔸X∗1\mathbb{A}_{X_{*}}^{1} over X∗X_{*} and such that the scheme-theoretic fiber π−1​(x0)\pi^{-1}\left(x_{0}\right) is nonempty and reduced, consisting of a disjoint union of curves isomorphic to the affine line 𝔸k1\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1}. A DFS with base (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right) is simply referred to as a Danielewski surface.

A morphism of Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces with base (X,x0)\left(X,x_{0}\right) is a birational XX-morphism β:S′→S\beta:S^{\prime}\rightarrow S restricting to an X∗X_{*}-isomorphism β∗:S′∣X∗⟶∼S∣X∗\beta_{*}:S^{\prime}\mid_{X_{*}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}S\mid_{X_{*}}.

Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces together with these morphisms form a sub-category 𝔇(A,x)\mathfrak{D}_{\left(A,x\right)} (or 𝔇(X,x0)\mathfrak{D}_{\left(X,x_{0}\right)}) of the category (Sch/X)\left(\textrm{Sch}_{/X}\right) of XX-schemes.

2.2.

The total space SS of DFS π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X is a smooth affine surface over kk. Indeed, X/kX/k is itself affine and smooth, and the local criterion for flatness ([2, III,§5]) guarantees that π\pi is a faithfully flat morphism, whence a smooth morphism as its geometric fibers are regular. Note that in contrast with general DFS’s, a Danielewski surface is an affine kk-scheme of finite type since in this case X≃𝔸k1X\simeq\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1} by definition. In general, an arbitrary 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π:S→𝔸k1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{k}^{1} on a smooth affine surface SS does not give rise to a structure of Danielewski surface on SS, but this does not prevent SS from being a Danielewski surface for another suitable 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. For instance, the Bandman and Makar-Limanov surface [1] S⊂Spec​(k⁡[x]​[y,z,u])S\subset\textrm{Spec}\left(k\left[x\right]\left[y,z,u\right]\right) with equations

x​z−y⁡(y−1)=0,y​u−z2=0,x​u−(y−1)​z=0,xz-y\left(y-1\right)=0,\quad yu-z^{2}=0,\quad xu-\left(y-1\right)z=0,

equipped with the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration p​ru:S→Spec​(k⁡[u])pr_{u}:S\rightarrow\textrm{Spec}\left(k\left[u\right]\right) is not a Danielewski surface with base (k⁡[u],u)\left(k\left[u\right],u\right). Indeed the fiber p​ru−1​(0)pr_{u}^{-1}\left(0\right) is not reduced. However, it is a Danielewski surface p​rx:S→Spec​(k⁡[x])pr_{x}:S\rightarrow\textrm{Spec}\left(k\left[x\right]\right) with base (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right).

Following Fieseler [7], DFS’s with base (X,x0)\left(X,x_{0}\right) can be described as certain 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundles ρ:S→Y\rho:S\rightarrow Y over a curve δ:Y→X\delta:Y\rightarrow X with an nn-fold point over x0x_{0}. In this section, we give a new interpretation of Fieseler’s ’cocycle construction’.

Torsors under a line bundle

Given an invertible sheaf ℒ\mathcal{L} on a scheme XX, the line bundle

𝐕⁡(ℒ)=𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜⁡(𝐒⁡(ℒ))=𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜⁡(⨁n≥0ℒn)⟶X\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)=\mathbf{Spec}\left(\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)\right)=\mathbf{Spec}\left(\bigoplus_{n\geq 0}\mathcal{L}^{n}\right)\longrightarrow X

is equipped with the structure of a commutative group scheme for the group law m:𝐕⁡(ℒ)×X𝐕⁡(ℒ)→𝐕⁡(ℒ)m:\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)\times_{X}\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)\rightarrow\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right) defined by means of the 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-algebras homomorphism 𝐒⁡(ℒ)⟶𝐒⁡(ℒ)⊗𝐒⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)\longrightarrow\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)\otimes\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\right) induced by the diagonal homomorphism Δ:ℒ→ℒ⊕ℒ\Delta:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{L}\oplus\mathcal{L}. For instance, if ℒ=𝒪X\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{O}_{X} then 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right) is simply the additive group scheme 𝔾a,X=𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜⁡(𝒪X​[T])\mathbb{G}_{a,X}=\mathbf{Spec}\left(\mathcal{O}_{X}\left[T\right]\right).

2.3.

A scheme π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X locally isomorphic to the trivial line bundle 𝔸X1\mathbb{A}_{X}^{1} is called an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle. If SS comes further equipped with an action of a line bundle 𝐕⁡(ℒ)/X\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)/X for which there exists an open covering 𝒰=(Xi)i∈I\mathcal{U}=\left(X_{i}\right)_{i\in I} of XX such that S∣XiS\mid_{X_{i}} is equivariantly isomorphic to 𝐕⁡(ℒ)∣Xi\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)\mid_{X_{i}} acting on itself by translations for every i∈Ii\in I, then we say that SS is a 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)-torsor. We recall [9, XI.4.7] that the set of isomorphism classes of 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)-torsors is a group isomorphic to H1​(X,ℒ∨)H^{1}\left(X,\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right). Indeed, an automorphism of the symmetric 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-algebra 𝐒⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\right) is equivariant for the co-action of 𝐒⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\right) on itself by translations if and only if it is induced by an homomorphism of 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-modules (g,Id):ℒ→𝒪X⊕ℒ\left(g,\textrm{Id}\right):\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{X}\oplus\mathcal{L}, where g∈HomX​(ℒ,𝒪X)g\in\textrm{Hom}_{X}\left(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{O}_{X}\right). Therefore, given a 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)-torsor π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X which becomes trivial on 𝒰\mathcal{U}, there exists a Čech cocycle g={gi​j}i,j∈I∈C1​(𝒰,ℒ∨)g=\left\{g_{ij}\right\}_{i,j\in I}\in C^{1}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right) such that SS is isomorphic to the scheme 𝐖⁡(𝒰,ℒ,g)\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L},g\right) defined as the spectrum of the quasi-coherent 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-algebra obtained by gluing the symmetric algebras 𝐒⁡(ℒ∣Xi)\mathbf{S}\left(\mathcal{L}\mid_{X_{i}}\right) over Xi​j=Xi∩XjX_{ij}=X_{i}\cap X_{j} by means of the 𝒪Xi​j\mathcal{O}_{X_{ij}}-algebras isomorphisms 𝐒⁡(gi​j,Id)\mathbf{S}\left(g_{ij},\textrm{Id}\right) induced by the 𝒪Xi​j\mathcal{O}_{X_{ij}}-modules homomorphisms (gi​j,Id)∈HomXi​j​(ℒ∣Xi​j,𝒪Xi​j⊕ℒ∣Xi​j)\left(g_{ij},\textrm{Id}\right)\in\textrm{Hom}_{X_{ij}}\left(\mathcal{L}\mid_{X_{ij}},\mathcal{O}_{X_{ij}}\oplus\mathcal{L}\mid_{X_{ij}}\right), i≠ji\neq j. The isomorphism class of 𝐖⁡(𝒰,ℒ,g)\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L},g\right) is simply the image in H1​(X,ℒ∨)≃Hˇ1​(X,ℒ∨)H^{1}\left(X,\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right)\simeq\check{H}^{1}\left(X,\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right) of the class [g]∈Hˇ1​(𝒰,ℒ∨)\left[g\right]\in\check{H}^{1}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right) of g∈C1​(𝒰,ℒ∨)g\in C^{1}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right).

2.4.

If the base scheme XX is integral, then every 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X admits a structure of a 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)-torsor for a suitable invertible sheaf ℒ\mathcal{L} on XX. Indeed, since XX is integral, the transition isomorphisms τi​j=τi∘τj−1\tau_{ij}=\tau_{i}\circ\tau_{j}^{-1} associated with a given collection of trivialisations τi:S∣Xi→∼Spec​(𝒪Xi​[T])\tau_{i}:S\mid_{X_{i}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathcal{O}_{X_{i}}\left[T\right]\right), i∈Ii\in I, are induced by automorphisms T↦g~i​j+fi​j​TT\mapsto\tilde{g}_{ij}+f_{ij}T of 𝒪Xi​j​[T]\mathcal{O}_{X_{ij}}\left[T\right], where g~i​j∈Γ⁡(Xi​j,𝒪X)\tilde{g}_{ij}\in\Gamma\left(X_{ij},\mathcal{O}_{X}\right) and fi​j∈Γ⁡(Xi​j,𝒪X∗)f_{ij}\in\Gamma\left(X_{ij},\mathcal{O}_{X}^{*}\right). For a triple of indices i≠j≠ki\neq j\neq k, the identity τi​k=τj​k∘τi​j\tau_{ik}=\tau_{jk}\circ\tau_{ij} over Xi∩Xj∩XkX_{i}\cap X_{j}\cap X_{k} guarantees that (fi​j)i,j∈I∈C1​(𝒰,𝒪X∗)\left(f_{ij}\right)_{i,j\in I}\in C^{1}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{O}_{X}^{*}\right) is a Čech cocycle defining an invertible sheaf ℒ\mathcal{L} on XX, trivial on 𝒰\mathcal{U}, with isomorphisms ϕi:ℒ∣Xi→∼𝒪Xi\phi_{i}:\mathcal{L}\mid_{X_{i}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{O}_{X_{i}}, i∈Ii\in I. By construction, g={g~i​j⋅ϕi∣Xi​j}i,j∈I∈C1​(𝒰,ℒ∨)g=\left\{\tilde{g}_{ij}\cdot\phi_{i}\mid_{X_{ij}}\right\}_{i,j\in I}\in C^{1}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L}^{\vee}\right) is a Čech cocycle for which SS is XX-isomorphic to the 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)-torsor 𝐖⁡(𝒰,ℒ,g)\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L},g\right).

Schemes with an nn-fold divisor

Given a principal divisor x0=div​(x)x_{0}=\textrm{div}\left(x\right) on an integral scheme XX and an integer n≥1n\geq 1, we let δn:X⁡(n)=X⁡(x0,n)→X\delta_{n}:X\left(n\right)=X\left(x_{0},n\right)\rightarrow X be the scheme obtained by gluing nn copies di:Xi​(n)→∼Xd_{i}:X_{i}\left(n\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}X of XX by the identity over the open subsets Xi​(n)∗=Xi​(n)∖xi​(n)X_{i}\left(n\right)_{*}=X_{i}\left(n\right)\setminus x_{i}\left(n\right), where xi​(n)=di−1​(x0)x_{i}\left(n\right)=d_{i}^{-1}\left(x_{0}\right). We denote by 𝒰(n)=(Xi​(n))i=1,…,n\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)}=\left(X_{i}\left(n\right)\right)_{i=1,\ldots,n} the canonical open covering of X⁡(n)X\left(n\right). For every i≠ji\neq j, we let Xi​j​(n)=Xi​(n)∩Xj​(n)≃X∖{x0}X_{ij}\left(n\right)=X_{i}\left(n\right)\cap X_{j}\left(n\right)\simeq X\setminus\left\{x_{0}\right\}.

Definition 2.5.

Given a multi-index μ=(μ1,…,μn)∈ℤn\mu=\left(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, we let

ℒn,μ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu} =\displaystyle= 𝒪X⁡(n)​(μ1​x1​(n)+…+μn​xn​(n))\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{X\left(n\right)}\left(\mu_{1}x_{1}\left(n\right)+\ldots+\mu_{n}x_{n}\left(n\right)\right)

be sub-𝒪X⁡(n)\mathcal{O}_{X\left(n\right)}-module of the constant sheaf 𝒦X⁡(n)\mathcal{K}_{X\left(n\right)} of rational functions on X⁡(n)X\left(n\right) generated by (x∘δn)−μi\left(x\circ\delta_{n}\right)^{-\mu_{i}} on Xi​(n)X_{i}\left(n\right). The dual sheaf ℒn,μ∨\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu}^{\vee} of ℒn,μ\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu} is isomorphic to the sheaf ℒn,−μ\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu} corresponding to the multi-index −μ=(−μ1,…,−μn)∈ℤn-\mu=\left(-\mu_{1},\ldots,-\mu_{n}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. We denote by sμs_{\mu} the canonical rational section of ℒn,μ\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu} corresponding to the constant section 1∈Γ⁡(X⁡(n),𝒦X⁡(n))1\in\Gamma\left(X\left(n\right),\mathcal{K}_{X\left(n\right)}\right).

Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces as torsors

Given a DFS π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X with base (X,x0)\left(X,x_{0}\right), we denote by C1,…,CnC_{1},\ldots,C_{n} the connected component of the fiber π−1​(x0)\pi^{-1}\left(x_{0}\right). We let δn:X⁡(n)=X⁡(x0,n)→X\delta_{n}:X\left(n\right)=X\left(x_{0},n\right)\rightarrow X be as above, and we let ρn:S→X⁡(n)\rho_{n}:S\rightarrow X\left(n\right) be the unique XX-morphism such that π=δn∘ρn\pi=\delta_{n}\circ\rho_{n}, and such that Ci=ρn−1​(xi​(n))C_{i}=\rho_{n}^{-1}\left(x_{i}\left(n\right)\right) for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

Proposition 2.6.

There exist a multi-index μ=(μ1,…,μn,)∈ℤ≥0n\mu=\left(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{n,}\right)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n} such that μi=0\mu_{i}=0 for at least one indice ii, and a cocycle g∈C1​(𝒰(n),ℒn,μ)g\in C^{1}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)},\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu}\right) such that SS is X⁡(n)X\left(n\right)-isomorphic to the 𝐕⁡(ℒn,−μ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu}\right)-torsor ρn:𝐖⁡(𝒰(n),ℒn,−μ,g)→X⁡(n)\rho_{n}:\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)},\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu},g\right)\rightarrow X\left(n\right).

Proof.

Since XX is either the affine line or the spectrum of a discrete valuation ring, the Picard group Pic​(X)\textrm{Pic}\left(X\right) is trivial, and so every invertible sheaf on X⁡(n)X\left(n\right) is isomorphic to ℒn,−μ\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu} for a certain multi-index μ∈ℤ≥0n\mu\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n} such that μi=0\mu_{i}=0 for at least one indice ii. Moreover, every open subset Xi​(n)≃XX_{i}\left(n\right)\simeq X of the covering 𝒰(n)\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)} is affine. Therefore, a 𝐕⁡(ℒn,−μ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu}\right)-torsor ρ:W→X⁡(n)\rho:W\rightarrow X\left(n\right) is isomorphic to 𝐖⁡(𝒰(n),ℒn,−μ,g)\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)},\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu},g\right) for a certain cocycle g∈C1​(𝒰,ℒn,μ)g\in C^{1}\left(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu}\right) representing its isomorphism class c⁡(W)∈H1​(X⁡(n),ℒn,μ)c\left(W\right)\in H^{1}\left(X\left(n\right),\mathcal{L}_{n,\mu}\right). So, by (2.4), it suffices to show that ρn:S→X⁡(n)\rho_{n}:S\rightarrow X\left(n\right) is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle . This can be done in a similar way as in Lemma 1.2 in [7]. ∎

2.7.

In view of the correspondence (2.4) between 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundles and 𝐕⁡(ℒ)\mathbf{V}\left(\mathcal{L}\right)-torsors, a DFS 𝐖⁡(𝒰(n),ℒn,−μ,g)\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)},\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu},g\right) is XX-isomorphic to the surface S=⨆i=1n𝔸Xi1/∼S=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{A}_{X_{i}}^{1}/\sim obtained by gluing nn copies of 𝔸Xi1=Spec​(A⁡[Ti])\mathbb{A}_{X_{i}}^{1}=\textrm{Spec}\left(A\left[T_{i}\right]\right) of 𝔸X1\mathbb{A}_{X}^{1} by means of AxA_{x}-algebras isomorphisms Ax​[Ti]→∼Ax​[Tj]A_{x}\left[T_{i}\right]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\rightarrow}}A_{x}\left[T_{j}\right], Ti↦g~i​j+xμi−μj​TjT_{i}\mapsto\tilde{g}_{ij}+x^{\mu_{i}-\mu_{j}}T_{j}, where g~i​j:=xμi​gi​j∈Ax\tilde{g}_{ij}:=x^{\mu_{i}}g_{ij}\in A_{x} for every i≠ji\neq j. In this way, we recover the ”cocycle construction” of Fieseler [7] .

2.8.

A general scheme S=𝐖⁡(𝒰(n),ℒn,−μ,g)S=\mathbf{W}\left(\mathcal{U}_{\left(n\right)},\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu},g\right) is not affine. 3. Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces and labelled rooted trees

Here we give a combinatorial description of DFS’s by means of labelled trees. To state the main result of this section, we need the following definition.

Definition 3.1.

A relative Danielewski-Fieseler surface with base (A,x)\left(A,x\right) is a morphism 𝔖=(ψ:S→𝔸X1)\mathfrak{S}=\left(\psi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{X}^{1}\right) of DFS’s with base (A,x)\left(A,x\right). A morphism of relative DFS’s is a morphism of DFS’s β:S′→S\beta:S^{\prime}\rightarrow S such that ψ′=ψ∘β\psi^{\prime}=\psi\circ\beta.

This section is devoted to the proof of the following result.

Theorem 3.2.

The category 𝔇→(A,x)\overrightarrow{\mathfrak{D}}_{\left(A,x\right)} of relative DFS’s with base (A,x)\left(A,x\right) is equivalent to the category 𝒯(A,x)\mathcal{T}_{\left(A,x\right)} of (A,x)\left(A,x\right)-labelled rooted trees.

In the following subsections, we construct an equivalence of categories in the form of a covariant functor 𝔖:𝒯(A,x)→𝔇→/(A,x)\mathfrak{S}:\mathcal{T}_{\left(A,x\right)}\rightarrow\overrightarrow{\mathfrak{D}}_{/\left(A,x\right)}.

4. Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces and affine modifications

Here we exploit the structure of rooted trees to give another description of morphisms of DFS’s. As a consequence, we obtain a canonical procedure to construct an open embedding of a DFS π:S→X\pi:S\rightarrow X into a projective XX-scheme π¯:S¯→X\bar{\pi}:\bar{S}\rightarrow X.

Every morphism of Danielewski-Fieseler surfaces factors into a finite sequence of fibered modifications followed by an open embedding.

5. Danielewski surfaces

We recall (2.1) that a Danielewski surface is a DFS with base (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right), where kk denotes a field of caracteristic zero. As a consequence of (1.6) and (3.2), the category 𝔇→(k⁡[x],x)\overrightarrow{\mathfrak{D}}_{\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)} of relative Danielewski surfaces is equivalent to the category 𝒯wk\mathcal{T}_{w}^{k} of fine kk-weighted trees. Therefore, every isomorphism class in 𝔇→(k⁡[x],x)\overrightarrow{\mathfrak{D}}_{\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)} contains a canonical object (ψ0:S0→𝔸X1)\left(\psi_{0}:S_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{X}^{1}\right), consisting of the canonical morphism of the DFS π:S0=S⁡(γw)→X\pi:S_{0}=S\left(\gamma_{w}\right)\rightarrow X defined by the (k⁡[x],x)\left(k\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled tree γw\gamma_{w} obtain from a fine kk-weighted tree by the procedure described in (1.6). In this section, we characterize Danielewski surfaces with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant in case that the base field kk is algebraically closed.

Notation 5.1.

Throughout this section, k¯\bar{k} denotes an algebraically closed field of caracteristic zero.

Normal affine surfaces with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant

The Makar-Limanov invariant [10] of an affine algebraic variety V=Spec​(B)V=\textrm{Spec}\left(B\right) over k¯\bar{k} is the sub-algebra ML​(V)\textrm{ML}\left(V\right) of BB consisting of regular functions on VV which are invariant under all 𝔾a,k\mathbb{G}_{a,k}-action on VV. If ML​(V)=k¯\textrm{ML}\left(V\right)=\bar{k}, then we say that VV has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant. It is known that a normal affine surface surface SS has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant if and only if it admits two 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations π1:S→X1≃𝔸k¯1\pi_{1}:S\rightarrow X_{1}\simeq\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{1} and π2:S→X2≃𝔸k¯1\pi_{2}:S\rightarrow X_{2}\simeq\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{1} with distinct general fibers. This property leads a geometrical criterion for SS to have trivial Makar-Limanov invariant. We recall that a minimal completion of SS is an open embedding S↪S¯S\hookrightarrow\bar{S} of SS into a normal projective surface S¯\bar{S}, nonsingular along B=S¯∖SB=\bar{S}\setminus S, such that BB is an S​N​CSNC-divisor, with nonsingular curves as irreducible components, which does not contain (−1)\left(-1\right)-curves meeting at most two other components transversally in a single point. In [6], the author established that a complex normal affine surface SS has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant if and only if the dual graph of the boundary divisor of any minimal completion of SS is a chain. Since the arguments given in Proposition 2.10 and Theorem 2.16 in [6] remain valid over an arbitrary algebraically closed field of caracteristic zero, we obtain the following more general criterion.

Theorem 5.2.

A normal affine surface S≄Spec​(k¯​[x,x−1,y])S\not\simeq\textrm{Spec}\left(\bar{k}\left[x,x^{-1},y\right]\right) has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant if and only if the dual graph of the boundary divisor of every minimal completion of SS is a chain. Moreover, if there exists a completion of SS with this property, then this also holds for every other minimal completion.

Danielewski surfaces with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant

Here we apply the general criterion (5.2) to Danielewski surfaces.

Definition 5.3.

A comb is a rooted tree Γ\Gamma such that Γ∖L⁡(Γ)\Gamma\setminus L\left(\Gamma\right) is a chain. Equivalently, Γ\Gamma is a comb if every e∈Γ∖L⁡(Γ)e\in\Gamma\setminus L\left(\Gamma\right) has at most one child which is not a leaf of Γ\Gamma. For instance, the tree Γ\Gamma of Figure 11 is a comb rooted in e0e_{0}.

For Danielewski surfaces

A Danielewski surface S/k¯S/\bar{k} has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant if and only if it is isomorphic to a Danielewski surface S⁡(γ)S\left(\gamma\right) defined by an (k¯​[x],x)\left(\bar{k}\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled comb γ\gamma.

In [5], we prove that a Danielewski surface with base (k¯​[x],x)\left(\bar{k}\left[x\right],x\right) has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant if and only if it is isomorphic to a surface SP1,…,PnS_{P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}}.

Corollary 5.6.

Given a morphism a Danielewski surfaces β:S′→S\beta:S^{\prime}\rightarrow S , we let

be the factorization of β\beta into a sequence of fibered modifications followed by an open immersion. Then the following hold.

The Makar-Limanov invariant of Sk0S_{k_{0}} being trivial, we can suppose that Sk0S_{k_{0}} is isomorphic to the surface defined by a (k¯​[x],x)\left(\bar{k}\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled comb γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right). Then Sk0−1S_{k_{0}-1} is isomorphic to the surface defined by a comb obtained from γ\gamma by blowing-down the leaves at the unique maximal element ee of Γ∖Leaves​(Γ)\Gamma\setminus\textrm{Leaves}\left(\Gamma\right). Thus Sk0−1S_{k_{0}-1} has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant by virtue of (5.4), and so, (a) follows by induction. To prove (b), we can again suppose that S≃S⁡(γ)S\simeq S\left(\gamma\right) for a certain (k¯​[x],x)\left(\bar{k}\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled comb γ=(Γ,σ)\gamma=\left(\Gamma,\sigma\right). As a consequence of the above description, we recover the characterization of the Danielewski surfaces SP,1={xz−P(y)=0}S_{P,1}=\left\{xz-P\left(y\right)=0\right\} in 𝔸k¯3=Spec​(k¯​[x,y,z])\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{3}=\textrm{Spec}\left(\bar{k}\left[x,y,z\right]\right) given in [1].

Corollary 5.7.

For a Danielewski surface π:S→𝔸k¯1\pi:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{1}, the following are equivalent.

a) ML​(S)=k¯\textrm{ML}\left(S\right)=\bar{k} and the canonical sheaf ωS\omega_{S} of SS is trivial

b) S≃S⁡(γ)S\simeq S\left(\gamma\right) for a suitable (k¯​[x],x)\left(\bar{k}\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled comb γ\gamma of height h≤1h\leq 1.

c) S≃SP,1⊂𝔸k¯3S\simeq S_{P,1}\subset\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{3} for a certain nonconstant polynomial PP with simple roots.

Proof.

By (3.10), we can suppose that S=S⁡(γ)S=S\left(\gamma\right) for a certain essential (k¯​[x],x)\left(\bar{k}\left[x\right],x\right)-labelled tree γ\gamma. The canonical sheaf ωS⁡(γ)\omega_{S\left(\gamma\right)} is trivial if and only if if and only if the invertible sheaf ℒn,−μ⁡(γ)\mathcal{L}_{n,-\mu\left(\gamma\right)} on X⁡(n)X\left(n\right) is trivial (see the proof of (2.13)). By construction, this is the case if and only if all the leaves of γ\gamma are at the same level. On the other hand, by (5.2), ML​(S​(γ))\textrm{ML}\left(S\left(\gamma\right)\right) is trivial if and only γ\gamma is a comb. Thus (a) and (b) are equivalent since an essential comb with all its leaves at the same level is either the trivial tree or a nontrivial comb of height 11. Finally, (b) and (c) are equivalent by virtue of (3.5). ∎

Cyclic quotients of Danielewski surfaces

A closed fiber Sz0S_{z_{0}} of an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→Zq:S\rightarrow Z on a normal affine surface is called degenerate if it is not isomorphic to 𝔸k⁡(z0)1\mathbb{A}_{k\left(z_{0}\right)}^{1}. In [7], Fieseler describes the structure of invariant neighbourhoods of degenerate fibers of a quotient 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→Z=S//𝔾a,ℂq:S\rightarrow Z=S//\mathbb{G}_{a,\mathbb{C}} on a normal affine surface S/ℂS/\mathbb{C} with a nontrivial 𝔾a,ℂ\mathbb{G}_{a,\mathbb{C}}-action. This description, which remains valid for affine surfaces defined over an algebraically closed field of caracteristic zero, can be reinterpreted as follows.

Proposition 5.8.

Let q:S→Zq:S\rightarrow Z be an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration on a normal affine surface S/k¯S/\bar{k}. If Sz0=q−1​(z0)S_{z_{0}}=q^{-1}\left(z_{0}\right) is a degenerate fiber of qq, then there exist a finite morphism ϕ:X→Z′=Spec​(𝒪Z,z0)\phi:X\rightarrow Z^{\prime}=\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathcal{O}_{Z,z_{0}}\right) totally ramified at the unique point x0x_{0} over z0z_{0} and a DFS π:S~→X\pi:\tilde{S}\rightarrow X with base (X,x0)\left(X,x_{0}\right) equipped with an action of a cyclic group ℤm\mathbb{Z}_{m} such that S×ZZ′=S~/ℤmS\times_{Z}Z^{\prime}=\tilde{S}/\mathbb{Z}_{m}.

Proof.

If Sz0S_{z_{0}} is reduced then every irreducible component of Sz0S_{z_{0}} is a connected component of Sz0S_{z_{0}} and is isomorphic to 𝔸k¯1\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{1} (see Lemma 1.2 in [7]). Thus p2:S′=S×ZZ′→Z′p_{2}:S^{\prime}=S\times_{Z}Z^{\prime}\rightarrow Z^{\prime} is already a DFS with base (Z′,z0)\left(Z^{\prime},z_{0}\right). Otherwise, if Sz0S_{z_{0}} is irreducible but not reduced, say with multiplicity m≥2m\geq 2, then, by Theorem 1.7 in [7], there exists a Galois covering ϕ:X→Z′\phi:X\rightarrow Z^{\prime} of order mm, étale over Z′∖{z0}Z^{\prime}\setminus\left\{z_{0}\right\} and totally ramified at the unique point x0x_{0} over z0z_{0}, such that the normalization S~\tilde{S} of (S′×Z′X)red\left(S^{\prime}\times_{Z^{\prime}}X\right)_{\textrm{red}} is a DFS π:S~→X\pi:\tilde{S}\rightarrow X, equipped with an action of the Galois group ℤm\mathbb{Z}_{m} of the covering ϕ\phi such that S′≃S~/ℤmS^{\prime}\simeq\tilde{S}/\mathbb{Z}_{m}. If Sz0S_{z_{0}} is neither irreducible nor reduced, with irreducible components CiC_{i} of multiplicity mi≥1m_{i}\geq 1, i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, then there exist DFS’s πi:S~i→Xi\pi_{i}:\tilde{S}_{i}\rightarrow X_{i} as above such that Si′=(S′∖Sz0)∪CiS^{\prime}_{i}=\left(S^{\prime}\setminus S_{z_{0}}\right)\cup C_{i} is isomorphic to S~i/ℤmi\tilde{S}_{i}/\mathbb{Z}_{m_{i}} for every i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. Letting mm be a common multiple of the mim_{i}’s, these DFS’s glue in a similar way as in the proof of Theorem 1.8 in [7] to a DFS π:S~→Y\pi:\tilde{S}\rightarrow Y, equipped with an action of ℤm\mathbb{Z}_{m} such that S′≃S~/ℤmS^{\prime}\simeq\tilde{S}/\mathbb{Z}_{m}. This completes the proof. ∎

The above description is local in nature. However, a similar argument shows that a surface S/k¯S/\bar{k} equipped with an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→𝔸k¯1q:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{1} with at most one degenerate fiber is isomorphic to cyclic quotient of a Danielewski surface. By Proposition 2.15 in [6], a normal affine surface S/k¯S/\bar{k} with a trivial Makar-Limanov admits an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration q:S→𝔸k¯1q:S\rightarrow\mathbb{A}_{\bar{k}}^{1} with this property. So we obtain the following result.

Theorem 5.9.

A normal affine surface S/k¯S/\bar{k} with a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant is isomorphic to a cyclic quotient of a Danielewski surface.

If the corresponding quotient morphism ψ:S′→S′/ℤm≃S\psi:S^{\prime}\rightarrow S^{\prime}/\mathbb{Z}_{m}\simeq S is étale in codimension 11, then the Danielewski surface S′S^{\prime} has a trivial Makar-Limanov invariant too (see e.g. [15]) . In general this is not the case, as shown by the following example.

Example 5.10.

A similar argument as in (3.5) shows that the Danielewski surface with base (ℂ⁡[x],x)\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x\right],x\right) defined by the following labelled tree

-2.2,-1)(8,1.2)

is isomorphic to the surface p​rx:S′→Spec​(ℂ⁡[x])pr_{x}:S^{\prime}\rightarrow\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x\right]\right) in 𝔸ℂ4=Spec​(ℂ⁡[x,y,z,u])\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{C}}^{4}=\textrm{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}\left[x,y,z,u\right]\right) given by the equations
